Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Physiotherapy helps arthritis by providing a comprehensive assessment, exercise programmes, and manual therapy. Physiotherapists offer pain management advice, joint protection techniques, and gait re-training. You can access physiotherapy on the NHS via GP referral or self-referral, or privately. Your first appointment includes assessment, physical examination, and a personalised treatment plan.

If there is one healthcare professional every person with arthritis should know about, it is a physiotherapist. Physiotherapy is a cornerstone of arthritis treatment — recommended by NICE as a first-line approach for osteoarthritis, and a vital part of the multidisciplinary care recommended for rheumatoid arthritis. This guide explains exactly what physio can do for your joints, how to access it on the NHS, what private treatment costs, and what to expect at your first appointment.

What Can a Physiotherapist Do for Arthritis?

A physiotherapist is a movement and rehabilitation expert. They do far more than hand you a sheet of exercises. Their role includes: comprehensive assessment (looking at your whole body — how you walk, sit, stand, what muscles are weak or tight), exercise prescription (a personalised programme for your body, your joints, and your goals), manual therapy (hands-on techniques to mobilise stiff joints and release tight muscles), pain management advice (education on pacing, flare management, and using movement to reduce pain), joint protection techniques (teaching you how to move in ways that reduce strain on damaged joints), gait re-training (improving how you walk to reduce joint stress), and referral and liaison (connecting you with occupational therapy, orthopaedics, pain management programmes). UK physiotherapists are regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) and are often members of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP). You are in safe hands.

Types of Physiotherapy for Arthritis

Exercise-based physiotherapy is the bread and butter of arthritis care — your physio designs a programme of strengthening, flexibility, and balance exercises tailored to your joints and fitness level. Manual therapy involves hands-on joint mobilisation (gentle, controlled movements) and soft-tissue massage — providing short-term relief and helping you move more freely. Some NHS physiotherapists are trained in acupuncture — evidence for arthritis is mixed but some people find it helps. Electrotherapy (ultrasound, laser) is sometimes used though the evidence base is limited. Perhaps most importantly, education and self-management — your physio teaches you about your condition and gives you tools to manage it yourself, for life.

How to Get Physiotherapy on the NHS

There are two main routes. Route 1 — GP referral: your GP refers you to your local NHS physiotherapy service. The physiotherapy department contacts you with an appointment. Route 2 — NHS MSK self-referral: in many parts of the UK, you can refer yourself directly to an NHS musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy service — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and takes pressure off GP surgeries.

NHS MSK Self-Referral — How It Works

Self-referral (also called "self-refer" or "direct access") is available in many areas of England, Scotland, and Wales. Here is how: 1) Find your local service — search online for "NHS physiotherapy self-referral [your area]" or check your GP practice website. 2) Complete a form — usually online but sometimes by phone — answering questions about your symptoms, general health, and what you need help with. 3) Triage — a physiotherapist reviews your form and decides if physiotherapy is appropriate and how quickly you need to be seen. 4) Appointment — if accepted, you receive an appointment, usually within a few weeks. Most adults with muscle or joint problems can self-refer. NHS physiotherapy is free at the point of use.

Private Physiotherapy — Costs and What to Expect

If NHS waiting times are long in your area or you want more frequent sessions, private physiotherapy is an option. Initial assessment costs £45–£80 and follow-up sessions cost £40–£65. Many clinics offer packages (e.g., 6 sessions for a reduced rate). Some health insurance policies cover physiotherapy. Look for HCPC registration (mandatory) and CSP membership with specialist interests (e.g., arthritis, rheumatology). The CSP "Physio2U" directory and "Physio First" network are good places to search. Private sessions usually offer longer appointments (45–60 minutes vs 20–30 minutes on NHS), more flexibility on appointment times (evenings, weekends), and continuity (same physio every time).

Hydrotherapy for Arthritis

Hydrotherapy (aquatic physiotherapy) is performed in a warm-water pool (usually 33–36°C) with a physiotherapist guiding specific exercises. It is not just swimming. The water's buoyancy supports body weight, reducing stress on joints. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases stiffness. Moving through water strengthens muscles gently. Hydrotherapy is ideal if land-based exercise is too painful. Research shows it reduces pain and improves function in both OA and RA. It is available on the NHS in some areas (usually hospital physiotherapy departments), though access varies. Private hydrotherapy sessions cost £50–£80.

What to Expect at Your First Physio Appointment

Before you go: wear loose comfortable clothing, bring a list of your medications, and think about your goals (what would you like to be able to do that you cannot do now?). During the appointment (45–60 minutes): conversation about your pain, general health, work, hobbies, and what matters to you; physical assessment — you may be asked to walk, sit, stand, and perform simple movements — the physio may gently feel your joints and test strength and range of motion (you can stop at any time); explanation of findings; and together you agree on a treatment plan — exercises, goals, and follow-up appointments. After: you will usually leave with 2–4 exercises to practise. Consistency is everything. Follow-up sessions every 2–4 weeks to check progress.

Practical next steps for Physiotherapy for Arthritis — How It Helps and How to Access It

If you came here about Physiotherapy for Arthritis — How It Helps and How to Access It, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Physiotherapy Arthritis Helps Access

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
